t:
(a) 
Section 1000 (e) of the Internal Revenue Code (relating to certain discretionary trusts) is hereby amended by striking out “prior to January 1, 1945,” and inserting in lieu thereof “on or before December 31, 1947 (or on a later date in any case where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioner, in accordance with regulations prescribed by him with the approval of the Secretary, that failure to relinquish prior to such later date was for reasonable cause)“.
 
    (b) 

If any amount paid prior to the date of the enactment of this joint resolution constitutes an overpayment of gift tax solely by reason of the amendment made by this section, no interest shall be allowed or paid with respect to the amount of such overpayment.

fable.w: The amendment contemplates the Commissioner prescribing regulations governing when a late relinquishment is for reasonable cause, and a grant of regulatory authority counts as rulemaking and therefore as participation under the definition. The tempting reading is that this is only a technical tax amendment with intra-government approval (Commissioner and Secretary) and an individual taxpayer showing, neither of which is participation on its own. That reading fails because the section relies on regulations being prescribed, which is the rulemaking trigger.
fable.s: in accordance with regulations prescribed by him with the approval of the Secretary

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to change a deadline for discretionary trusts. It mentions regulations prescribed by the Commissioner with the approval of the Secretary, but this is internal administrative procedure between federal officials. There is no requirement for consultation with outside parties, public comment, or advisory boards involving non-federal members. The interaction described is strictly within the federal government.
qwen_block.s: Section 1000 (e) of the Internal Revenue Code (relating to certain discretionary trusts) is hereby amended by striking out “prior to January 1, 1945,” and inserting in lieu thereof “on or before December 31, 1947 (or on a later date in any case where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioner, in accordance with regulations prescribed by him with the approval of the Secretary, that failure to relinquish prior to such later date was for reasonable cause)“.

opus.w: The section requires the Commissioner to issue regulations governing how taxpayers show reasonable cause for a late relinquishment. Under the definition and Example 6, a requirement or grant of authority to make rules counts as participation, because rulemaking gives the public a chance to comment. The tempting 'No' reading treats the Secretary's approval as the only interaction, and that approval is indeed inside the federal government. But the rulemaking itself is what triggers the 'Yes'.
opus.s: in accordance with regulations prescribed by him with the approval of the Secretary
opus.b:
1. **The tempting "No" reading.** The section reads like a technical tax amendment, and the only interaction it names is between the Commissioner and the Secretary. That approval step stays inside the federal government, so on its own it is not participation.
2. **Why that reading fails.** The definition says "Yes" whenever a section requires rulemaking. Example 6 counts even a discretionary grant of power to regulate. Here, whether a late relinquishment had "reasonable cause" must be shown "in accordance with regulations prescribed by him." That is a rulemaking requirement, and rulemaking brings in public notice and comment.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends tax code provisions regarding discretionary trusts and gift tax overpayments. The process described involves a taxpayer showing cause to the Commissioner for a later date, which is an administrative determination of individual tax liability or refund eligibility, not a participatory process involving consultation with outside parties before a federal decision. The 'approval of the Secretary' is intra-governmental coordination. The definition excludes applications for benefits or standard administrative adjudications.
qwen_chat.s: on or before December 31, 1947 (or on a later date in any case where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioner, in accordance with regulations prescribed by him with the approval of the Secretary, that failure to relinquish prior to such later date was for reasonable cause)
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the phrase "shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioner" implies a process where an outside party (the taxpayer) participates by providing evidence. However, this is a standard administrative procedure for determining tax liability or refunds, not a participatory mechanism in the sense of consulting with outsiders before making a policy or regulatory decision. It is essentially an application for a waiver or exception based on specific facts, which falls under the "applications for benefits" trap or simply standard administrative adjudication, not the defined "participation" (consultation/coordination with outsiders before a decision). The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits. Furthermore, the "approval of the Secretary" mentioned is intra-governmental (Commissioner and Secretary are both federal officials).
